# ECSS-E-HB-20-07A, "Electromagnetic compatibility handbook", 5 September 2012

**What this file is.** A transcription of the clauses this project CITES, not a copy of the handbook. The
document is published free of charge by the European Cooperation for Space Standardization and is fetched,
never redistributed here; what follows is section 6.1.2, the part that is about a printed circuit board, with
enough surrounding text to show what each statement is and is not. Anything this project does not use is not
reproduced.

**What it is in the ECSS hierarchy, which decides how much weight it carries.** Its own foreword: *"This
Handbook is one document of the series of ECSS Documents intended to be used as supporting material for ECSS
Standards in space projects and applications ... The material in this Handbook is defined in terms of
description and recommendation how to organize and perform the work of ECSS-E-ST-20-07C."* So it is a
HANDBOOK and not a standard: it recommends and explains, it does not levy requirements. A number taken from it
is an authority for a mechanism and a magnitude, never a shall.

## 6.1.2.2 Spectrum of a trapezoidal periodic signal

A periodic digital signal is approximated as a trapezoid of amplitude V0, period Tp, pulse width tpw and rise
time tr, with f0 = 1/Tp the fundamental. For a symmetrical signal with equal rise and fall times the nth
harmonic is

    Vn = V0 * [sin(pi n f0 tpw) / (pi n f0 tpw)] * [sin(pi n f0 tr) / (pi n f0 tr)]

and *"the spectrum is bounded by the envelope shown in Figure 6-2, which has the following break points"*:

    F1 = 1 / (pi * tpw)        F2 = 1 / (pi * tr)

*"The spacing between lines is 2f0 = 2/Tp for a perfectly symmetrical signal (only odd harmonics). In the
general case, the spacing is f0. The envelope can be a sufficient approximation of the spectrum at high
frequency."* Above F2 the envelope falls at 40 dB per decade; between F1 and F2 at 20 dB per decade.

**This is the clause this project uses for the BANDWIDTH OF AN EDGE.** The highest frequency that a signal
puts on a conductor in any quantity is F2 = 1/(pi tr), from the rise time and from nothing else: not from the
clock rate, not from the data rate. A 12 Mbit/s bus driven by a 1 ns edge carries energy to 318 MHz.

## 6.1.2.3 Introductory example (a real case, the handbook's words)

A clock from an FPGA to an ADC, 35 mm of track on the top layer, 6 pF of load: *"f0 = 872 kHz, V0 = 5 V (i.e.
134 dBuV), tr = 200 ps"*, so *"F1 = 1/(pi tpw) = 555 kHz, F2 = 1/(pi tr) = 1.6 GHz"*, and the peak charging
current is *"Imax = (5 V / 0.2 ns) x 6 pF = 150 mA"*. Measured radiated emission at 1 m appears at 1.4 GHz.
The differential-mode estimate uses the small loop of the track and its image in the plane:

    E = 0.013 * I * A * F(MHz)^2 / D = 0.013 * I * l * 2h * F(MHz)^2 / D

*"where l = 35 mm (track length approximately lambda/6 in this example), h = 0,5 mm, D is the observation
distance"*, giving about 40 dBuV/m at 1 m. The handbook's conclusion, verbatim:

> This example shows that with steep clock edges and no precaution, a short track can be "sufficient" to
> result in excessive radiated emission in a protected frequency band, even if the fundamental frequency of
> the clock is low.

The fix in the example was not a shorter track: a 1 kOhm series resistor with the track's own capacitance,
which took Imax from 150 mA to 5 mA and put the emission below the noise floor.

**What this project takes from it.** Two things and no more: that the length that matters is measured against
the wavelength at F2 rather than at the clock rate, and that a track at lambda/6 of that frequency is already
a textbook radiator. It is a worked example, not a limit: **the handbook states no numeric critical length**,
so a project that wants one states its own criterion and says so.

## 6.1.2.5.1 Components

> Therefore the following recommendation should be followed:
> * Avoid using faster devices than needed, i.e. use fast switching components only if dictated by timing
>   requirements;
> * Use SMT as far as possible;
> * Prefer IC packages with a large number of power and ground pins, rather placed in the centre of the
>   package.

## 6.1.2.5.2 PCB design techniques

> In general, the following practices are recommended:
> * Limitation of tracks length for clocks;
> * Use of tracks with controlled characteristic impedance:
>   * Microstrips or striplines;
>   * Matched terminations.
> * Ground (and power) planes over the whole surface of each PCB:
>   * Slots or gaps in ground (and power) planes crossed by clock tracks lead to the generation of common
>     mode currents, which increase the radiated emission dramatically;
>   * The capacitance between power and ground planes (if on adjacent layers) can be a more effective source
>     of current for the fast components than decoupling capacitors at high frequencies (UHF); it is a
>     (small) decoupling capacitance with very low inductance.
> * Minimisation of changes of layer for clock tracks;
> * No clock tracks close to the edge of a PCB;
> * Clocks routed on a layer adjacent to a solid (not split) ground or power plane, with minimisation of the
>   clock track height above the plane (this avoids an increase of the plane net partial inductance and of
>   the resulting voltage drop);
> * Embedding of clock tracks:
>   * The stripline configuration results in approximately 20 dB lower emissions than microstrip;
>   * For a microstrip, 97% of the return current is contained in a distance of +- 20 times the height of
>     the trace above the plane, whereas for a stripline, 99% of the return current of contained in a
>     distance of +- 3 times the height of the trace above the plane.

The last figure is attributed to reference [12], H.W. Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering", 2009.
The trace-to-edge rule is supported in the same handbook's reference list by [33], Marco Leone, "Design
Expressions for the Trace-to-Edge Common-Mode Inductance of a Printed Circuit Board", IEEE Transactions on
EMC.

**This is the clause this project uses for the RETURN PATH.** It says three separate things that a tool can
be held to: a fast track runs adjacent to a SOLID plane, a gap in that plane crossed by a fast track is a
common-mode source, and the return current of a microstrip spreads +- 20 h laterally (97 percent) against
+- 3 h for a stripline (99 percent). The third gives the width a reference has to have under a track to count
as a reference at all, and it is a property of the stackup rather than of the net.

## 6.1.2.5.3 Equipment design

> In order to limit the cables excitation by the voltage drops along the PCB ground planes, and therefore the
> (CM) radiated emission by the cables, it is important to ensure a good PCB ground plane continuity to the
> chassis, especially in the I/O connector zone.

## What this handbook does NOT say, recorded so nobody cites it for these

* **No numeric critical length and no transmission-line threshold.** It gives the bandwidth of an edge and one
  worked example at lambda/6. Any "a net longer than X is a transmission line" in this project is this
  project's own criterion, stated with its reason.
* **No per-class tolerance** for how far a fast net may run without an adjacent reference. The handbook's
  position is that it should not happen at all for a clock.
* **No PCB creepage or clearance table.** That is ECSS-Q-ST-70-12C and, for high voltage, ECSS-E-HB-20-05A.
* **No decoupling loop-area limit in millimetres.** It says the plane pair beats the capacitors at UHF.
* It is written for spacecraft equipment in a shielded enclosure, so its emission levels and test limits are
  not this kit's; what transfers is the physics and the design practice, not the limits.

## Books it rests on, for anyone checking a number

* [12] H.W. Ott, "Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering", September 2009, ISBN-13 978-0470189306.
* [14] S. Caniggia and F. Maradei, "Signal Integrity and Radiated Emission of High-Speed Digital Systems",
  November 2008, ISBN-13 978-0470511664.
* [32] M. Mardiguian, "Controlling radiated emissions by design", Kluwer Academic Publishers, 2nd revised
  edition, December 2000, ISBN-13 978-0792379782.

None of the three is in this tree and none is free; they are named because the handbook names them as the
source of the figures above.
